SM16L-01.free_elimination: none. Checked: all four options are congruent to 2 mod 3, so the 'answer is 3x-4, so it must be 3k-4' residue argument kills nothing. No magnitude bound is readable without collecting the terms, and no two options stand in a printed relation. Author's 'none found' confirmed.
SM16L-01.note: Clean. The residue closure (every option of the form 3k-4) is the one thing that could have leaked here and it is intact - whether by design or luck, it is the right property. Distractors 14/17 are the two half-distribution errors and 32 the sign error; all three prose paths reproduce their printed values exactly.

SM16L-02.free_elimination: SIGN/MAGNITUDE, 1 struck. Every printed option exceeds 3, so (x-3)/5 is positive for all of them; the stem subtracts that positive quantity from (x+3)/2 to reach 9, hence (x+3)/2 > 9 and x > 15. 14 dies. Free: deciding the sign of the second term and halving 18 is not the same act as clearing the denominators.
SM16L-02.note: Author declared none; one is live. 1-of-3 is inside normal SAT tolerance (the real test prints options below the key routinely), so this is a note not a drop. 14 is also the weakest distractor conceptually - 'multiply the right side by 2+5=7' is a rarer error than the other two. Notation: the stem prints fractions inline as (x+3)/2; the digital SAT stacks them. Batch-level rendering question, not an item defect.

SM16L-03.free_elimination: TWO mechanisms, 2 struck solidly and a 3rd conditionally. (a) One subtraction of the printed equations gives x + 3y = 57 - not a solve, since a second combination is still needed - and if x > 0 then y < 19, killing 19 and 21. 19 requires exactly x = 0 and 21 requires x = -6. (b) 4x + 5y = 123 is odd, so with integer x, 5y and hence y must be odd: 12 dies. Both lean on conventions the stem never states (x positive, x integer), which is why I count 2 rather than 3.
SM16L-03.note: HOLD candidate. The one-subtraction bound is the concerning one: subtracting the two printed equations is the first thing a student does anyway, and it hands over an upper bound on y that only the key survives once you add the usual positivity assumption. 12 is additionally the x-value, the most-guessed distractor family. Stem says 'the system of equations above' - legacy paper-SAT phrasing; the digital test does not say 'above'.

SM16L-04.free_elimination: none that is arithmetic-free. The strongest shortcut is a weighted-average read: 4560/260 is about 17.5, nearer 20 than 12, so more than half of 260 are adult, i.e. x > 130 - which leaves only 180. But that is one division, and the range argument (4560 sits 1440 above the 3120 all-student floor in a 2080-wide band) is literally the intended computation. Author's 'none found' stands under the strict test.
SM16L-04.note: Author graded hard; this is the canonical mixture word problem and belongs at medium. Worth recording that the key is the only option above 130 = half the count, and half the count IS free - so the item rewards an estimator who can do one division. That is legitimate SAT skill, not a leak, but it is why this cannot carry a hard slot.

SM16L-05.free_elimination: none. Checked the residue closure: every option minus 33 is a multiple of 4 (32, 40, 52, 60), so a solver who recovers the slope 4 but not the run cannot narrow the set. No bound is readable without computing the slope.
SM16L-05.note: Clean, and the residue closure is intact for the same reason as item 01. The key is the smallest of the four - all three distractors over-count the run - which is a mild test-wiseness tell shared with items 11 and 13 (see batch note), not an in-item elimination.

SM16L-06.free_elimination: none. The option set contains 14 and 19, which differ by exactly the printed anchor x-coordinate 5, so a solver who knows the 'forgot to add the anchor' trap can read the pair and take the larger. That is a meta-tell about distractor conventions, not a bound on the item, and 31 = 14 + 17 sits in the same relation with the printed y-coordinate, which blunts it.
SM16L-06.note: Clean. The two anchor-offset pairs (19 = 14+5 and 31 = 14+17) actually protect each other: a solver reading the offset pattern cannot tell which coordinate was supposed to be added. Good distractor construction.

SM16L-07.second_defensible: 9 and 23 both satisfy the inequality; they are wrong only because they are not the LEAST such integer. That is the intended trap and matches real SAT practice, so exclusivity holds on the stem as written.
SM16L-07.free_elimination: none arithmetic-free. No adjacent pair is printed, so the 'least integer above' structure gives nothing away. A plug-in route exists (test 4, fails; test 7, works) and is cheap, but it is arithmetic and it is a legitimate solve path the real test also permits.
SM16L-07.note: Clean. Deliberately checked the adjacency structure the brief warns about - 4, 7, 9, 23 contains no adjacent pair, so the 'least integer' phrasing does not point at anything. The non-integer boundary 67/11 is the right choice; an integer boundary would have made the ceiling step invisible.

SM16L-08.free_elimination: THREE struck, not the one declared. (a) The author's declared kill is real: y >= 6 spends at least 8(6) = 48 of the 147 budget, leaving under 100 for 5x, so x < 20 and 29 dies with no arithmetic beyond 8x6. (b) UNDECLARED and larger: the stem asks for the GREATEST possible value, so a smaller option can only be correct if every larger option is infeasible. 12 and 14 are therefore never candidates until 19 is ruled out, and ruling 19 in is a single check (95 + 48 = 143 <= 147). The item collapses to 'test the options top-down', which is two checks against a four-step optimisation.
SM16L-08.note: HOLD. The author found the kill it had defended against and missed the one inherent to its own stem verb. Note this is a format exposure, not an authoring slip - every 'greatest possible value' multiple-choice item has it, and the real SAT mitigates it by asking these in the student-produced-response section. That is the honest fix here: this is the batch's only genuinely hard item and it wants an SPR slot, not four options. Notation: 'is less than or equal to' is spelled out in words; the digital SAT prints the symbols.

SM16L-09.free_elimination: DIVISIBILITY, 2 struck, and it is decisive. The longer piece L satisfies L = 3S - 8, so L + 8 = 3S must be divisible by 3 for an integer shorter piece. 61+8 = 69 and 67+8 = 75 pass; 71+8 = 79 and 83+8 = 91 fail. Completely free - one addition and a digit-sum - and it separates the key from 71, the nearest option, which is exactly where a guessing student would otherwise be stuck.
SM16L-09.note: DROP. The author declared 'none found'; this is the cleanest free elimination in the batch and it halves the field. It survives even the objection that lengths need not be integers, because a student applying the usual convention lands on the right answer. The 71 path is also the weakest prose in the batch: it moves the 8 to the wrong side to get s = 21 and then reports 92 - 21 rather than 3s - 8, switching which formula it trusts mid-error. Stated explicitly, so coherent, but contrived.

SM16L-10.free_elimination: RESIDUE / CLOSURE, ALL THREE struck, with no arithmetic whatsoever. The common total must be reachable by the SECOND plan as well: total = 102 + 25m, so its last two digits must be 02, 27, 52 or 77. 427 ends in 27. 414, 583 and 648 do not. A solver reads the final two digits of four numbers and is done. The author protected the first plan's closure and not the second's: every option IS 258 + 13m (m = 12, 13, 25, 30), so that half is airtight and the half nobody checked gives away the item.
SM16L-10.note: DROP - the worst item in the batch and a textbook instance of the declared-constraint failure mode. An item whose answer must satisfy TWO printed models needs both residues checked; only one was. Re-author rather than patch: shifting the distractors to 402/552/652 would be fitting to the instrument that caught it. Also demote from hard - break-even with an 'answer is the output not the input' twist is medium.

SM16L-11.free_elimination: MAGNITUDE, 2 struck. The constants are 97 and 143, so 10x cannot be far from 240; at x = 40 or 60 the term 10x (400, 600) dwarfs everything printed. More sharply, 6x > 0 forces 143 - 6x < 143, hence 10x < 240 and x < 24 - which kills 40 and 60 outright and makes 24 attainable only at x = 0. The exact ceiling 240/10 = 24 costs the same addition as the solve, so I count the two clear magnitude kills only.
SM16L-11.note: KEEP. This is the batch's only easy item and the exposure matters least here - a student who cannot do it in one line is not the student the item is for. But note the option set is {240/16, 240/10, 240/6, 240/4}: all four are 240 over something, which is the uniform brief discussed at batch level.

SM16L-12.free_elimination: THREE struck by two mechanisms. (a) The slope is 3/2, which is greater than 1, and the run from x = 6 to x = 24 is 18; so the rise exceeds 18 and w > 29. 20 and 23 die. Reading the slope is the skill the item tests, but it is not the same act as computing the rise, so this is free. (b) Weaker: the rise is (3/2)(18) = 3x9, a multiple of 3, so w - 11 must be divisible by 3. 30 - 11 = 19 fails. 30 therefore dies too, leaving the key alone.
SM16L-12.note: DROP, or hold for re-authoring. Both distractors below the key are shallower-than-1 slopes, and the moment a solver reads slope 3/2 off the standard form they are gone - the item's own first step destroys half the option set. Fixable in principle by placing distractors above 29, but re-author rather than patch. Demote from hard: slope-from-standard-form plus a parallel line plus a run is a routine three-step.

SM16L-13.free_elimination: none. Checked the residue closure: every option minus 37 is a multiple of 8 (88, 96, 112, 120), so all four are legal terms of some sequence with increment 8 through 37 and no divisibility argument narrows the set. Intact.
SM16L-13.note: Clean. The key is the smallest option because all three distractors over-count the gaps - a test-wiseness tell rather than an elimination, but it is the third item in the batch with that shape (see 05 and 11). One distractor straddling the key, from an under-count, would close it.

SM16L-14.free_elimination: SIGN, 1 struck. Expanding the right side gives kx + 18 = 9x + 54. The constant on the right is larger by 36, so with x positive the coefficient on the left must exceed 9 to compensate: k > 9. 7 dies. No arithmetic - it is a comparison of 18 against 54. 10 and 21 both survive, since nothing free pins k - 9 to exactly 6.
SM16L-14.note: KEEP. 1-of-3 is within tolerance and 7 is the weakest distractor anyway (the half-distribution error). Demote from hard: substituting a supplied solution and solving for the parameter is a standard medium. This is the only item in the batch where the unknown is not the variable, which is its real value - see batch note on the 01/02/11/14 cluster.
